It is Meccan, by the consensus of the scholars, with no disagreement that we know of.

Regarding the meaning of its nearness, there are two views:

The first: it is coming, and everything that is coming is near.

The second: because time, given how much has passed and how little remains, is near.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿while they are heedless﴾, that is, heedless of what God will do to them on that Day, ﴿turning away﴾ from preparing for it. It was also said: "The reckoning has drawn near for mankind" is general, while the heedlessness and turning away are specific to the disbelievers, as indicated by His saying: ﴿No reminder comes to them from their Lord, newly revealed﴾. Regarding this reminder there are three views:

The first: that it is the Qur'an, said by Ibn 'Abbas. According to this, the reference in "muhdath" (newly revealed) is to its being sent down, since it was revealed piece by piece.

The second: that it is a reminder among the reminders, and not the Qur'an, related by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi. Al-Naqqash said: it is a reminder from the Messenger of God, and not the Qur'an.

The third: that it is the Messenger of God, as evidenced by His saying in the context of the verse: ﴿Is this not but a human like yourselves?﴾, said by al-Hasan ibn al-Fadl.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They listen to it only while playing﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: they listen to the Qur'an mockingly.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿with hearts distracted﴾, that is, heedless of what is intended for them. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is: they listen to it only as players, with their hearts distracted; and it is permissible for it to be in the accusative, governed by His saying (p-340) ﴿playing﴾. 'Ikrimah, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Ibn Abi 'Ablah read "lahiyatun" in the nominative.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And they conferred secretly﴾, that is, they held private consultations among themselves, meaning the polytheists. Then He clarified who they were, saying: ﴿those who did wrong﴾, that is, who associated partners with God. "Alladhina" is in the nominative position as a substitute (badal) for the pronoun in "wa-asarru". Then He clarified the secret they conferred about, saying: ﴿Is this not but a human like yourselves?﴾, that is, a mortal, and not an angel. This is a denial of his prophethood. Some say that "asarru" here means "they revealed", since it is among the words with contrary meanings (adداd).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Will you then approach magic while you see?﴾, that is, will you accept magic, ﴿while you see﴾ that it is magic? They meant that following Muhammad ﷺ is following magic. ﴿He said: My Lord...﴾ Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, and Abu Bakr from 'Asim read "qul rabbi" (Say: My Lord). Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Hafs from 'Asim read "qala rabbi" (He said: My Lord), and it is so in the codices of the Kufans. This is in the form of a report, "from the Prophet ﷺ that he said". ﴿He knows the word﴾, that is, nothing that is said in the heavens and the earth is hidden from Him, so He knows what you conceal. ﴿Rather they said﴾: al-Farra' said: it is a rejection introduced by "bal" (rather), in terms of their denial, even though no statement of their denial preceded it; because its meaning is reporting about the deniers. Some of them said: what he brings is magic; some said: "confused dreams" (adghath ahlam), which are jumbled things seen in sleep, and we have explained them in (Yusuf: 44); some said: "he has fabricated it" (iftarahu), that is, invented it; and some said: he is a poet. ﴿So let him bring us a sign﴾ like the she-camel and the staff. They demanded signs after which there would be no respite.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿No town before them that We destroyed believed﴾, meaning the polytheists of Makkah. ﴿from a town﴾: the town is described, and what is meant is its people. The meaning is that the nations that were destroyed for denying the signs did not believe in the signs when they came to them; so how would these believe? Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 21, verse 16–24:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We did not create the heaven and the earth and what is between them in play.﴾ That is: We did not create that in vain. Rather, We created them as evidence of Our power and Our oneness, so that people would take heed from His creation and know that worship is fitting only for its Creator, and so that We may reward Our friends and punish Our enemies.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿If We had wished to take a pastime﴾ Regarding the occasion of its revelation there are two views:

The first: when the polytheists said, "The angels are the daughters of Allah, and the gods are His daughters," this verse was revealed. This was said by Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: the Christians of Najran said, "Isa is the son of Allah," so this verse was revealed. This was said by Muqatil.

Regarding the meaning of "pastime" (lahw) there are three views:

The first: a child. This was narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas, and al-Suddi also said so. al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is, "If We had wished to take a child who is a source of diversion by which We would be amused."

The second: a woman. This was narrated by 'Ata' from Ibn 'Abbas, and al-Hasan and Qatadah also said so. (p-344)

The third: play (al-la'ib). This was narrated by Ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn 'Abbas.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿We would have taken it from Us⟩ Ibn Juraij said: "We would have taken wives or a child from the inhabitants of the heaven, not from the inhabitants of the earth." Ibn Qutaybah said: The root of lahw is intercourse, and it was referred to by "lahw" just as it is referred to by "sirr" (secret). The meaning is: If We had done that, We would have taken it from Our presence, because you know that a man's child and his wife are with him, not with anyone else.

Regarding His saying, ﴿if We were to do so﴾ there are two views:

The first: that "in" (in) carries the meaning of "ma" (negation). This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan and Qatadah.

The second: that it carries the meaning of a condition. al-Zajjaj said: The meaning is, "If We were doing that — but We are not among those who do it." He said: The first view is the view of the exegetes, and the second is the view of the grammarians, and they also prefer the first view, because "in" can be in the place of negation, except that it most often comes with the lam. You say: "In kunta la-salihan," meaning: "You were only righteous."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Rather⟩ That is: leave aside what they said, for it is falsehood. ﴿We hurl the truth⟩ That is: We cast down the truth, which is the Qur'an, ﴿upon falsehood⟩ which is their lying, ﴿and it crushes it⟩ Ibn Qutaybah said: That is, it breaks it. The root of this is striking the brain with a blow, which is a fatal place. ﴿and behold, it vanishes⟩ That is: it perishes and goes away. The exegetes said: The meaning is that We nullify their lies by the truth We make clear, until it is extinguished. ﴿And woe to you for what you describe⟩ That is: for your describing Allah with what is not permissible. ﴿And to Him belongs whoever is in the heavens and the earth⟩ meaning: they are His servants and His possession. ﴿And those near Him⟩ meaning: the angels.

Regarding His saying, ﴿And they do not tire⟩ there are three views:

The first: they do not return. This was narrated by Ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn 'Abbas. (p-345)

The second: they do not cease. This was said by Mujahid. Ibn Qutaybah said: they do not grow weary; al-hasr is the one who stops and stands still from exhaustion and fatigue.

The third: they do not get bored. This was said by Ibn Zayd.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They do not slacken﴾ Qatadah said: they do not grow weary. Ka'b was asked: "Does not some matter occupy them? Does not some need occupy them?" He said to the questioner: "O my nephew, glorification has been made for them just as breathing has been made for you. This is a question in the sense of denial, and the meaning is: they have not taken gods that raise the dead. ﴿Had there been in them⟩ meaning: the heavens and the earth, ﴿gods⟩ meaning: worshipped ones, ﴿other than Allah⟩ al-Farra' said: "other than Allah," and al-Zajjaj said: "except Allah."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿they would have been ruined⟩ That is: they would have been destroyed and perished, and whoever is in them would have perished, because of the existence of mutual opposition among the gods, so the affairs of the world would not run in order. For every matter that proceeds from two or more is not free from disagreement.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿He is not questioned about what He does⟩ That is: about what He decrees concerning His servants of guidance and misguidance, honour and humiliation, because He is the Owner of creation, and creation will be questioned about their deeds, for they are servants who must obey the command of their Master. When He, Mighty and Majestic, had nullified, by reason, that there could be another god besides Him, by His saying "they would have been ruined," He nullified it also from the standpoint of command, so He said: ﴿Or have they taken gods besides Him?⟩ This is a question of denial and rebuke. ﴿Say: Bring your proof⟩ for what you say, ﴿This is the reminder of those with me⟩ meaning: the Qur'an is the report of those who are with me in my religion, from among those who follow me until the Day of Resurrection, with what they have of reward for obedience and punishment for disobedience. ﴿And the reminder of those before me⟩ meaning: the revealed books. The meaning is: this Qur'an and these books that were revealed before it — look, is there in any one of them that Allah commanded taking a god besides Him? Thus by this clarification the permissibility of taking another object of worship is nullified from the standpoint of command. al-Zajjaj said: It was said to them: Bring your proof that some messenger among the messengers informed his community that they had a god other than Allah.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Rather, most of them﴾ meaning: the disbelievers of Makkah, ﴿do not know the truth⟩ and concerning this there are two views:

The first: that it is the Qur'an, said by Ibn 'Abbas. The second: that it is monotheism (tawhid), said by Muqatil. "So they turn away" from reflection and contemplation, and from the faith that is obligatory upon them.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 21, verses 25–29:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿We sent no messenger before you except that We revealed to him﴾. Hamza, al-Kisa'i, and Hafs from ʿAsim read (nūḥī) with the nūn, while the rest read it with the yāʾ.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And they say, "The Most Merciful has taken to Himself a son."﴾ Concerning those who said this there are two views:

The first: they are the polytheists of Quraysh. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas. Ibn Ishaq said: the one who said this was al-Nadr ibn al-Harith.

The second: they are the Jews, who said: "God intermarried with the jinn, and from them came the angels." This was said by Qatadah. According to both views, the intended meaning of "son" is the angels. Likewise, the intended meaning of His saying ﴿Rather, they are honored servants﴾ is: rather, they are servants whom God has honored and chosen. ﴿They do not precede Him in speech﴾, meaning they do not speak except with what He commands them. Ibn Qutaybah said: they do not speak until He speaks, and then they speak after Him, and they do not act until He commands them.

It was also said: they do not seek forgiveness in this world. ﴿Except for one whom He approves﴾, meaning for one with whom He is pleased. ﴿And they are, out of fear of Him﴾, meaning out of their fear of Him, so the verbal noun is attributed to its object. ﴿Apprehensive﴾, meaning fearful. Al-Hasan said: trembling.

﴿And whoever among them says﴾, meaning among the angels. Al-Dahhak and others said: this is specific to Iblis; no one among the angels called anyone to worship himself besides him. Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi said: this is the view of those who say he was among the angels, for Iblis said this to the angels who descended with him to the earth. Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 21, verses 30–33:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Have not those who disbelieved seen﴾; that is: Have they not known? Ibn Kathir recited: (Alam yara alladhina kafaru), without the waw between the alif and the lam, and it is likewise written thus in the codices of the people of Makkah. ﴿That the heavens and the earth were a joined mass, and We separated them﴾. Abu Ubayda said: "as-samawat" is plural and "al-ard" is singular, so the adjective, which is in the plural form, came in the form of the singular adjective. The Arabs do this when they combine a plural with a singular. And ar-ratq is a verbal noun (masdar) which may be applied to the singular, the dual, and the plural, and to the masculine and the feminine alike. The meaning of ar-ratq is that which has no opening. Az-Zajjaj said: the meaning is that they were two things possessing ratq, and He made them two things possessing fatq. He did not say "ratqayn" because ar-ratq is a masdar.

The commentators have three views concerning its intended meaning:

The first: the heavens did not rain, and the earth did not produce vegetation, so He split the one with rain and the other with plants. This was narrated by Abdullah ibn Dinar from Ibn Abbas, and Ata, Ikrimah, Mujahid in one narration, and ad-Dahhak among others said likewise.

The second: the heavens and the earth were joined together, and Allah separated them. This was narrated by al-Awfi from Ibn Abbas, and al-Hasan, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, and Qatada said likewise.

The third: He split six earths from the earth so they became seven, and six heavens from the heaven so they became seven. This was narrated by as-Suddi from his shaykhs, and Ibn Abi Najih from Mujahid.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We made from water every living thing﴾. Mu'adh al-Qari, Ibn Abi Abla, and Humayd ibn Qays recited: (kulla shay'in hayyan), in the accusative.

Concerning this water there are two views:

One: it is the known water, and the meaning is: We made water a cause for the life of every living thing. This is what most of them said. The second: it is the semen-drop (nutfa), as said by Abu al-'Aliya.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We placed in the earth firm mountains﴾. We have explained it in (an-Nahl: 15).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We made in them﴾; that is, in the mountains, ﴿broad passages﴾. Abu Ubayda said: they are the paths. Az-Zajjaj said: al-fijaj is the plural of fajj, which is every opening between two mountains. The meaning of ﴿paths﴾ is: roads. Ibn Abbas said: We made roads through the mountains so that you may be guided to your destinations on journeys. The commentators said: His saying "paths" is an explanation of "broad passages" and a clarification that those passages are open and traversed, for a fajj may not be passable. ﴿And We made the heaven a protected ceiling﴾; that is, it is for the earth like a ceiling.

Concerning the meaning of ﴿protected﴾ there are two views:

One: by the stars from the devils, as said by Abu Salih from Ibn Abbas.

The second: protected from falling except by Allah's permission, as said by az-Zajjaj.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And they﴾ meaning the disbelievers of Makkah, ﴿from its signs﴾; that is, its sun, its moon and its stars. Al-Farra' said: Mujahid recited (ayatiha) in the singular, making the heaven with what is in it one sign, and both are correct.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Each﴾ meaning: the risers, ﴿in an orbit﴾. Ibn Qutayba said: the falak is the orbit of the stars that contains them, and it was called falak because of its circularity. From it is said: "falakat al-mighzal" (the whorl of the spindle), and "falaka thady al-mar'a" (the woman's breast became round). Abu Sulayman said: It has also been said that the falak, like the shape of a water-wheel's channel, is a circle beneath the heaven and above the earth; the earth is in its middle, and the sun, the moon, the stars, and night and day all move within the falak, and the falak does not turn them. The meaning of "yasbahun" is: they move along. Al-Farra' said: since swimming is an action of humans, it was mentioned with the nun (the masculine-plural form for rational beings), as in His saying: ﴿I saw them prostrating to me﴾ [Yusuf: 4], because prostration is an action of humans.

The first: the heavens did not rain, and the earth did not produce vegetation, so He split the one with rain and the other with plants. This was narrated by Abdullah ibn Dinar from Ibn Abbas, and Ata, Ikrimah, Mujahid in one narration, and ad-Dahhak among others said likewise.

The second: the heavens and the earth were joined together, and Allah separated them. This was narrated by al-Awfi from Ibn Abbas, and al-Hasan, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, and Qatada said likewise.

The third: He split six earths from the earth so they became seven, and six heavens from the heaven so they became seven. This was narrated by as-Suddi from his shaykhs, and Ibn Abi Najih from Mujahid.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We made from water every living thing﴾. Mu'adh al-Qari, Ibn Abi Abla, and Humayd ibn Qays recited: (kulla shay'in hayyan), in the accusative.

Concerning this water there are two views:

One: it is the known water, and the meaning is: We made water a cause for the life of every living thing. This is what most of them said. The second: it is the semen-drop (nutfa), as said by Abu al-'Aliya.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We placed in the earth firm mountains﴾. We have explained it in (an-Nahl: 15).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We made in them﴾; that is, in the mountains, ﴿broad passages﴾. Abu Ubayda said: they are the paths. Az-Zajjaj said: al-fijaj is the plural of fajj, which is every opening between two mountains. The meaning of ﴿paths﴾ is: roads. Ibn Abbas said: We made roads through the mountains so that you may be guided to your destinations on journeys. The commentators said: His saying "paths" is an explanation of "broad passages" and a clarification that those passages are open and traversed, for a fajj may not be passable. ﴿And We made the heaven a protected ceiling﴾; that is, it is for the earth like a ceiling.

Concerning the meaning of ﴿protected﴾ there are two views:

One: by the stars from the devils, as said by Abu Salih from Ibn Abbas.

The second: protected from falling except by Allah's permission, as said by az-Zajjaj.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And they﴾ meaning the disbelievers of Makkah, ﴿from its signs﴾; that is, its sun, its moon and its stars. Al-Farra' said: Mujahid recited (ayatiha) in the singular, making the heaven with what is in it one sign, and both are correct.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Each﴾ meaning: the risers, ﴿in an orbit﴾. Ibn Qutayba said: the falak is the orbit of the stars that contains them, and it was called falak because of its circularity. From it is said: "falakat al-mighzal" (the whorl of the spindle), and "falaka thady al-mar'a" (the woman's breast became round). Abu Sulayman said: It has also been said that the falak, like the shape of a water-wheel's channel, is a circle beneath the heaven and above the earth; the earth is in its middle, and the sun, the moon, the stars, and night and day all move within the falak, and the falak does not turn them. The meaning of "yasbahun" is: they move along. Al-Farra' said: since swimming is an action of humans, it was mentioned with the nun (the masculine-plural form for rational beings), as in His saying: ﴿I saw them prostrating to me﴾ [Yusuf: 4], because prostration is an action of humans.

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 21, verses 34–36:**

His words, exalted is He: ﴿We did not grant eternal life to any human before you﴾. The occasion of its revelation: some people said, "Muhammad will not die," so this verse was revealed. This is related by Muqatil. The meaning of the verse: We did not grant eternal life to anyone among the children of Adam before you. *Al-khuld* (eternal life) means lasting existence without end. "So if you die, will they be the immortals?" means the polytheists of Mecca, because they said: ﴿We await for him the misfortunes of time﴾ [Al-Tur: 30].

His words, exalted is He: ﴿And We test you with evil and with good﴾. Ibn Zayd said: We test you with what you love, to see how you give thanks, and with what you hate, to see how you endure patiently.

His words, exalted is He: ﴿And to Us you will be returned﴾. [Ibn ʿĀmir read *tarjiʿūn* with an open *tāʾ*. Ibn ʿAbbas related from Abu ʿAmr: *yarjiʿūn* with a *yāʾ* that is closed.] The rest read it with a closed *tāʾ*.

His words, exalted is He: ﴿And when those who disbelieved see you, they take you only in mockery﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: meaning the mockers. Al-Suddi said: it was revealed concerning Abu Jahl. The Messenger of Allah passed by him, and he laughed and said, "This is the prophet of the Banu ʿAbd Manaf." The word *in* here has the sense of *ma* (negation). The meaning of ﴿mockery﴾ is "one who is mocked." ﴿Is this the one who mentions your gods?﴾ That is, who speaks ill of your idols, and there is an implied "they say" within it. ﴿And they, at the mention of the Most Merciful, are disbelievers﴾. This is because they said, "We do not know the Most Merciful," so they disbelieved in the Most Merciful.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 21, verse 37–41:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Man was created of haste﴾. Abu Razin al-'Uqayli, Mujahid, and al-Dahhak recited (khalaqa al-insana) with a fatha on the kha and the lam and a nasb on the nun. This verse was revealed when the Quraysh were hasty for the punishment.

Regarding what is meant by "al-insan" (the human being) here, there are three opinions:

The first: al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, who is the one who said: ﴿O Allah, if this is indeed the truth from You...﴾ [al-Anfal: 32], narrated by 'Ata' from Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: Adam (peace be upon him), said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Suddi, and others.

The third: that it is a generic noun (ism jins), said by 'Ali ibn Ahmad al-Naysaburi. According to this, al-Nadr ibn al-Harith and others are included in it, even though the verse was revealed concerning him.

As for the one who says it refers to Adam, there are two opinions on the meaning of the statement:

One of them: he was created hasty. This is said by most scholars. According to this, it means: when Adam was molded with this trait, it was found in his offspring, and he bequeathed them haste.

The second: he was created from haste, meaning that his creation was hastened before sunset on Friday, the last of the six days. This is said by Mujahid.

As for the one who says it is a generic noun, there are two opinions on the meaning of the statement:

One of them: he was created hasty. al-Zajjaj said: the Arabs were addressed in terms they understand, and the Arabs say to one who plays excessively: "You were created only from play," intending exaggeration in describing him with that.

The second: that there is inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir) in the statement, and the meaning is: haste was created in the human being. This is said by Ibn Qutayba.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿I will show you My signs﴾. Concerning it there are two opinions:

One of them: what befell the earlier nations, meaning: you travel and see the traces of destruction among those who passed away. This is said by Ibn al-Sa'ib.

The second: that it is the killing at Badr. This is said by Muqatil.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So do not hasten Me﴾. Ya'qub kept the yaʾ in both states.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And they say, "When is this promise?"﴾ meaning: the Resurrection. ﴿If only those who disbelieved knew﴾ its answer is omitted, and the meaning is: if they knew the truth of the promise, they would not have hastened, ﴿when they will not ward off﴾; that is, they will not repel, ﴿from their faces the Fire﴾ ﴿when they enter it﴾, ﴿nor from their backs﴾, because it will encompass them, ﴿and they will not be helped﴾; that is, they will not be prevented from what has descended upon them. ﴿Rather, it will come upon them﴾, meaning: the Hour, ﴿suddenly﴾, unexpectedly, ﴿and it will confound them﴾, bewilder them. We have explained this at His saying: ﴿So the one who disbelieved was confounded﴾ [al-Baqarah: 258]. ﴿And they will not be able to avert it﴾; that is, to turn it away from them, nor will they be given respite for repentance or an excuse. Then He consoled His Prophet, saying: ﴿And messengers were certainly mocked before you﴾; that is, just as your people did to you, ﴿so there befell those who ridiculed them﴾; that is, descended upon, ﴿what they used to mock﴾, meaning: the punishment that they used to mock.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 21, verse 46–47:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We shall set up the scales of justice﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning is: "And We shall set up the scales possessing justice (dhawat al-qist)." Al-qist means justice, and it is a verbal noun (masdar) used as a description. It is said: "a scale that is just (mizan qist)," "two scales that are just (mizanan qist)," and "scales that are just (mawazin qist)." Al-Farra' said: "Al-qist is a description of the scales, even though it is in the singular, just as you say: 'You are justice ('adl),' and 'You are contentment (ridan).'" His saying: ﴿for the Day of Resurrection﴾, and "on the Day of Resurrection" (﴿sawa'in﴾). We have already discussed the matter of the scale at the beginning of al-A'raf (8).

If it is said: If the scale is one, what is the meaning of mentioning "scales" in the plural?

The answer: Since the deeds of creatures are weighed one portion after another, they are called "scales" (mawazin).

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So no soul will be wronged in anything﴾; that is, no doer of good will have any of his good deeds diminished, and no doer of evil will have his evil deeds increased. ﴿And if it should be the weight of a mustard seed﴾; that is, the weight of a grain. Nafi' read "mithqalu" (مِثْقالُ) with a raised lam (ḍamma). Al-Zajjaj said: The accusative "mithqala" (مِثْقالَ) is according to the meaning: "And if the deed should be the weight of a grain." Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: "And if the wrong should be the weight of a grain," because of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So no soul will be wronged in anything﴾. He said: Whoever reads with the raised form attributes the verb to "mithqal," just as it is attributed in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And if someone is in hardship﴾ [al-Baqarah: 280].

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿We bring it﴾; that is, We bring it. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, and Humayd read "atayna" (آتَيْنا) with a long vowel (mamdudatan); that is, We will requite it.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And sufficient are We as reckoners﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: It is in the accusative in two ways: one of them is as a specifier (tamyiz), and the second is as a circumstantial state (hal).

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 21, verses 48–50:

His statement, Exalted is He: ﴿And We certainly gave Moses and Aaron the Criterion﴾. Regarding this there are three opinions:

First: It is the Torah, through which one distinguishes between the lawful and the unlawful. This was said by Mujahid and Qatadah.

Second: It is the proof through which one distinguishes between the truth of Moses and the falsehood of Pharaoh. This was said by Ibn Zayd.

Third: It is the victory and deliverance granted to Moses, and the destruction of Pharaoh. This was said by Ibn al-Sa'ib.

His statement, Exalted is He: ﴿and a light﴾. Ikrimah narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he regarded the waw (and) here as superfluous (zaʾidah). Al-Zajjaj said: Some of the grammarians have said likewise, that the meaning is: "the Criterion is a light." But according to the Basran grammarians, the waw is not superfluous and does not occur except to mean conjunction (ʿatf). So here it is like His statement, Exalted is He: ﴿In it is guidance and light﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 44]. (p-356) The commentators said: The meaning is that they sought illumination through the Torah until they were guided by it in their religion. As for the meaning of His statement, Exalted is He: ﴿and a reminder for the God-fearing﴾, it is that they remember it and act by what is in it. ﴿Who fear their Lord unseen﴾. Regarding this there are four opinions:

First: They fear Him though they have not seen Him. This was said by the majority.

Second: They fear His punishment though they have not seen it. This was said by Muqatil.

Third: They fear Him where no one sees them. This was said by al-Zajjaj.

Fourth: They fear Him when they are absent from people's eyes, just as they fear Him when they are among people. This was said by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi.

Then he returned to mention the Qur'an, saying: ﴿And this﴾, meaning the Qur'an, is ﴿a reminder﴾ for whoever takes heed through it, and an admonition for whoever is admonished, ﴿blessed﴾, that is, abundant in good. ﴿Will you then deny it?﴾, O people of Makkah, that is, reject it? This is a question of reproach.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 21, verse 51–58:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We had already given Abraham his rushd (right guidance/maturity) before, and We were fully aware of him.﴾ That is, his guidance (hudahu). Concerning "from before" (min qabl), there are three opinions:

The first: from before his reaching maturity (bulugh). This was said by Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: We had granted him that in the prior knowledge (al-'ilm al-sabiq). This was said by al-Dahhak, from Ibn 'Abbas. (p-357)

The third: from before Moses and Aaron. This was said by al-Dahhak. We have already referred to the story of Abraham in (al-An'am: 75).

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and We were fully aware of him﴾ That is, We knew that he was a fitting recipient of the granting of rushd. Then He explained when He granted it to him, saying: ﴿When he said to his father and his people, "What are these statues (tamathil) to which you are devoted?"﴾ meaning: the idols (al-asnam). The word timthal (statue) is the name for a made object that is likened to one of God's creations, and its root is from "I made the thing like (mathaltu al-shay' bi-al-shay')", when I compare one thing to another. His saying: ﴿to which you are devoted (laha 'akifun)﴾ means: in worshipping them; ﴿devoted (akifun)﴾ means: remaining constantly. They answered him that they had seen their fathers worshipping them and so they followed them. He answered them that they and their fathers were in manifest error in what they did. ﴿They said, "Have you brought us the truth, or are you among the jesters?"﴾ meaning: "Are you in earnest, or are you joking?"

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿"By God, I will surely scheme against your idols"﴾ Kayd is the scheming of the schemer to harm the one he schemes against. He answered them that they and their fathers were in manifest error in what they did. ﴿They said, "Have you brought us the truth, or are you among the jesters?"﴾ meaning: "Are you in earnest, or are you joking?"

It is related that some Bedouin went out to seek provisions, and when they returned, a man secretly went during part of the night to the bag of his companion, took some grain from it, and put it into his own bag. When he wanted to leave and they both were tying up their bags, he saw his own bag becoming light while his companion's bag was becoming heavy. So he composed:

"A bag has covered some of the bags of the people; I have not seen a bag stealing before today."

Thus he accused his companion in a way subtler than explicit accusation.

Ibn al-Anbari said: Ibrahim's speech was true when examined, and the meaning of the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying, "Ibrahim told three lies," is: he said a statement that resembles a lie in appearance, but is not a lie.

'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may God be pleased with him, said: "It would not please me to possess, in exchange for what I know of the ma'arid of speech, the equivalent of my family and my wealth."

Al-Nakha'i said: They have a manner of speech which they use when they fear something, by which they ward off harm from themselves.

Ibn Sirin said: Speech is too broad for a witty person to need to lie.

The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to an old woman: "Indeed, old women will not enter Paradise," intending the verse: ﴿Indeed, We have produced them with a special production﴾ [al-Waqi'a: 35].

When Abu Bakr came out of the cave with the Messenger of God (ﷺ), whenever anyone asked him, "Who is this before you?" he would say: "A guide who guides me."

She said: "I believe in God, and I disbelieve my eyes." She went to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and informed him, and he laughed and was pleased with what she did.

**Ibn al-Jawzi, Zad al-Masir, on Surah 21, verses 64–67:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So they returned to themselves﴾. On this there are two views:

The first: some of them turned back to others. The second: each one of them turned back to himself, reflecting.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, it is you who are the wrongdoers﴾. On this there are five views:

The first: when you worship that which does not speak. This was said by Ibn Abbas.

The second: when you leave your gods alone and go away. This was said by Wahb ibn Munabbih.

The third: in worshipping these lesser ones alongside this great one. This is also related from Wahb.

The fourth: said to Abraham when you accused him while the axe was in the hand of the largest of the idols. This was said by Ibn Ishaq and Muqatil.

The fifth: "You are the wrongdoers toward Abraham" when you asked him while these idols of yours are present; ask them. This was mentioned by Ibn Jarir (al-Tabari).

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Then they were overturned upon their heads﴾. Abu Razin al-Uqayli, Ibn Abi Abla and Abu Haywa read *nukkisu* (نُكِّسُوا) with a raised *nun* and a *kasra* on the *kaf*, with the *kaf* doubled. Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Ibn Ya'mur and Asim al-Jahdari read *nakasu* (نَكَسُوا) with a *fatha* on the *nun* and on the *kaf*, with the *kaf* undoubled (p-365). Abu Ubayda said: ﴿nukisu﴾ means they were turned over. You say: "I overturned so-and-so on his head," when you overpower him and rise above him.

Then, regarding the intended meaning of this reversal, there are three views:

The first: bewilderment overtook them, so they said: ﴿Indeed you know that these do not speak﴾. This was said by Qatada.

The second: they returned to the first thing by which they used to describe them, that they do not speak. This was said by Ibn Qutayba.

The third: they turned against Abraham, arguing against him after they had acknowledged (the truth) to him, and they blamed themselves for accusing him. This was said by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi.

In his saying ﴿Indeed you know﴾ there is an implied ﴿they said﴾. In this there is an admission from them of the inability of what they worship to speak. At that point the proof was directed at Abraham, and he said, rebuking them: ﴿Do you worship, besides Allah, that which can neither benefit you nor harm you?﴾; that is, it does not provide for you or give you anything, ﴿nor harm you﴾ if you do not worship it. In this there is an exhortation to them to worship the One who possesses benefit and harm. ﴿Fie upon you (uffin lakum)﴾: al-Zajjaj said its meaning is: "Foulness to you." When he had placed the proof upon them, they became angry and said: "Burn him!"

It is mentioned in the tafsir (exegesis) that Namrud consulted them: "With what punishment shall I punish him?" A man said: "Burn him." So Allah caused the earth to swallow him, and he continues to sink and churn within it until the Day of Resurrection.

The Allusion to the Story

The people of tafsir (exegesis) mention that they imprisoned Ibrahim (peace be upon him) in a building, then they built for him a pit (ḥayr) whose wall was sixty cubits long, up to the foot of a towering mountain. The king's herald proclaimed: "O people, gather firewood for Ibrahim, and let no one, young or old, stay behind from this; whoever stays behind will be cast into that fire." They did this for forty nights, to the point that a woman would say: "If I succeed in such-and-such, I will certainly gather wood for the fire of Ibrahim." When the firewood reached the top of the wall, they sealed the doors of the pit and threw the fire into it. Its flame rose high, so that a bird passing over it would burn from the intensity of its heat. Then they built a towering structure, and on top of it they built a catapult (manjanīq), and they raised Ibrahim onto the top of the structure. Ibrahim raised his head to the sky and said: "O Allah, You are the One in the heaven, and I am the one on the earth; there is no one on the earth who worships You besides me. Allah is sufficient for me, and He is the best Disposer of affairs." The sky, the earth, the mountains and the angels said: "Our Lord, Ibrahim is being burned for You; permit us to help him." He said: "I know better about him; and if he calls upon you, then help him." They cast him into the fire when he was sixteen years old; it was also said twenty-six. He said: "Allah is sufficient for me, and He is the best Disposer of affairs." Jibril met him and said: "O Ibrahim, do you have any need?" He said: "As for you, no." Jibril said: "Then ask your Lord." He said: "My knowledge of my condition is sufficient for me in place of my asking." Then Allah, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿O fire, be coolness and safety upon Ibrahim﴾. Thus no fire on the face of the earth that day remained but was extinguished, and it thought that it had been addressed. Al-Suddi claimed that it was Jibril who called to it. Ibn 'Abbas said: "Had He not followed its coolness with safety, Ibrahim would have died from its cold." Al-Suddi said: "The angels took hold of Ibrahim's armpits and seated him on the ground, and behold, there was a spring of sweet water, and red roses and narcissus." Ka'b and Wahb said: "The fire burned nothing of Ibrahim except his bonds, and he remained in that place for seven days." Others said: "forty or fifty days." Then Jibril descended with a garment from Paradise and a rug (ṭanfasa) from Paradise; he clothed him in the garment and seated him upon the rug, and sat with him, conversing with him. It is also said that Azar came to Nimrod and said: "Permit me to bring out the bones of Ibrahim so that I may bury them." Nimrod set out and the people with him, and he ordered the wall to be breached. Behold, Ibrahim was in a garden, swaying, his garments dripping, wearing the garment with the rug beneath him, and the angel at his side. Nimrod called out to him: "O Ibrahim, your God whose power has reached this, is indeed great; are you able to come out?" He said: "Yes." Ibrahim got up, walking until he came out. He said: "Who was that I saw with you?" He said: "An angel whom my Lord sent to me to keep me company." Nimrod said: "I will offer a sacrifice (qurbān) to your God, because of what I have seen of His power." He said: "In that case, Allah will not accept from you what you have been upon of your religion." Nimrod said: "O Ibrahim, I cannot abandon my kingdom, but I will slaughter for Him." So he slaughtered the sacrifice and refrained from Ibrahim.

The exegetes said: The meaning of ﴿be coolness﴾ is: be of coolness; and ﴿safety﴾ means: safety. ﴿And they intended a scheme against him﴾, which was burning him with fire. ﴿So We made them the greatest losers﴾, which is that Allah, exalted, set gnats upon them, until it ate their flesh and drank their blood, and one entered the brain of Nimrod until it destroyed him. The meaning is: they plotted evil against him, and the evil turned back upon them.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We delivered him﴾; that is, from Nimrod and his scheme; ﴿and Lot﴾, who was the son of Ibrahim's brother, namely Lot son of Haran son of Terah, who had believed in him; so the two of them emigrated from the land of Iraq to al-Sham. Sarah was with Ibrahim according to the view of Wahb. Al-Suddi said: she was the daughter of the king of Harran; Ibrahim met her and married her on condition that he would not change her religion, and she had criticised her people for their religion.

As for His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿to the land which We have blessed﴾, there are two views concerning it:

One: that it is the land of al-Sham, and this is the view of the majority. Its blessing is that Allah, mighty and majestic, sent most of the prophets from it, and made abundant in it fertility, fruits and rivers.

The second: that it is Makkah, narrated by al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas; and the first is more sound.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We bestowed upon him﴾, meaning Ibrahim, ﴿Isaac and Jacob as an additional gift (nāfila)﴾. Concerning the meaning of nāfila there are two views:

One: that it means an increase, and what is intended by it is Jacob specifically, as though he asked for one and was given two. This is the position of Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, Ibn Zayd and al-Farra'.

The second: that nāfila means a gift, and what is intended is Isaac and Jacob. This is the position of Mujahid and 'Ata'.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And all We made righteous﴾, meaning Ibrahim, Isaac and Jacob. Abu 'Ubayda said: "kull" (all) may take a predicate in the singular form, because its wording is singular, and it may take a predicate in the plural form, because its meaning is plural.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We made them leaders (a'imma)﴾; that is, chiefs who are followed in goodness, ﴿guiding by Our command﴾; that is, calling people to Our religion by Our command to them to do so, ﴿and We revealed to them the doing of good deeds (fi'l al-khayrat)﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: the laws of prophethood. Muqatil said: righteous deeds. ﴿And the establishment of prayer (iqam al-salat)﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: omitting the ha' from (iqamat al-salat) is rare in the language; one says aqama iqamatan, and the omission is permissible because the idafa (annexation) is a substitute for the ha'.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 21, verses 78–82:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And David and Solomon, when they judged concerning the tilth﴾. Regarding it there are two opinions: (p-371)

One of them: it was a vineyard. This was said by Ibn Mas'ud, Masruq, and Shurayh.

The second: it was a field of crops. This was said by Qatadah.

﴿When the sheep of the people grazed in it by night﴾. Ibn Qutaybah said: that is, they grazed at night. It is said: "the sheep strayed (nafashat) at night," and they are called "nafash," "nuffash," and "nifash" (plural forms of camels or flocks that graze at night), and the singular is "nafish." Grazing by day is called "sarahat" and "sarabat." Qatadah said: nafsh is by night, and hamal is by day. Ibn al-Sikkit said: nafsh is when the sheep spread out at night and graze without a shepherd.

Indication of the story

The exegetes mention that two men were in the time of David, peace be upon him: one was the owner of a field, and the other the owner of sheep. The sheep broke loose and fell into the field, and left nothing of it. They brought their dispute to David, and he said to the owner of the field: "You shall have the sheep as compensation." Solomon said: "Is there not something other than that?" He said: "What is it?" He said: "The owners of the field take the sheep and benefit from their milk and their uses, and the owners of the sheep work the vineyard, until when it is like the night the sheep grazed in it, these give back to those their sheep, and those give back to these their vineyard." David said: "You have hit upon the right judgment," and then he ruled accordingly. That is His saying: ﴿And We were witnesses to their judgment﴾.

Regarding those referred to there are two opinions:

One: David and Solomon, and He mentioned them with the plural form, because two is a plural. This is the saying of al-Farra'.

The second: they are David, Solomon, and the litigants. This was said by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi. Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, and Ibn Abi 'Ablah recited: ﴿And We were witnesses to their judgment﴾ in the dual form. The meaning of (p-372) ﴿witnesses﴾ is that nothing of their affair was hidden from Us.

The meaning of ﴿that it may protect you﴾ is: that it may secure and shield you ﴿from your violence﴾, meaning war.

The exegetes said: they used to dive in the sea and extract pearls, ﴿and did other work besides that﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is: other than that. ﴿And We were guardians over them﴾, lest they corrupt what they did. Others said: lest they depart from his command.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 21, verses 78–82:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And David and Solomon, when they judged concerning the tilth﴾. Regarding it there are two opinions: (p-371)

One of them: it was a vineyard. This was said by Ibn Mas'ud, Masruq, and Shurayh.

The second: it was a field of crops. This was said by Qatadah.

﴿When the sheep of the people grazed in it by night﴾. Ibn Qutaybah said: that is, they grazed at night. It is said: "the sheep strayed (nafashat) at night," and they are called "nafash," "nuffash," and "nifash" (plural forms of camels or flocks that graze at night), and the singular is "nafish." Grazing by day is called "sarahat" and "sarabat." Qatadah said: nafsh is by night, and hamal is by day. Ibn al-Sikkit said: nafsh is when the sheep spread out at night and graze without a shepherd.

Indication of the story

The exegetes mention that two men were in the time of David, peace be upon him: one was the owner of a field, and the other the owner of sheep. The sheep broke loose and fell into the field, and left nothing of it. They brought their dispute to David, and he said to the owner of the field: "You shall have the sheep as compensation." Solomon said: "Is there not something other than that?" He said: "What is it?" He said: "The owners of the field take the sheep and benefit from their milk and their uses, and the owners of the sheep work the vineyard, until when it is like the night the sheep grazed in it, these give back to those their sheep, and those give back to these their vineyard." David said: "You have hit upon the right judgment," and then he ruled accordingly. That is His saying: ﴿And We were witnesses to their judgment﴾.

Regarding those referred to there are two opinions:

One: David and Solomon, and He mentioned them with the plural form, because two is a plural. This is the saying of al-Farra'.

The second: they are David, Solomon, and the litigants. This was said by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi. Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, and Ibn Abi 'Ablah recited: ﴿And We were witnesses to their judgment﴾ in the dual form. The meaning of (p-372) ﴿witnesses﴾ is that nothing of their affair was hidden from Us.

﴿So We gave understanding of it to Solomon﴾, meaning the case and the judgment. It was referred to by pronoun because what indicates it had already preceded in the mention of the judgment. ﴿And to each﴾ of them ﴿We gave judgment and knowledge﴾, and its explanation has already preceded. Al-Hasan said: Were it not for this verse, you would think that judges had perished; but He praised Solomon for his correctness and excused David for his effort (ijtihad).

Section

Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi said: The judgment of David and Solomon was entirely by way of ijtihad, and was not an explicit text; for if it had been an explicit text, they would not have disagreed. Qadi Abu Ya'la said: People have differed concerning sheep that graze at night in a man's field and damage it. The school of our companions holds that the owner is liable for compensation, and this is the saying of al-Shafi'i. Abu Hanifah and his companions said: there is no liability on him, by night or by day, unless the owner himself released them. The apparent meaning of the verse supports the view of our companions, because David ruled for compensation, and the law of those before us is law for us as long as its abrogation is not established. If it is said: the abrogation of this ruling is established, because David ruled for handing over the sheep to the owner of the field, and Solomon ruled that he should have their young and their wool, and there is no disagreement that whoever's sheep graze in a man's field owes nothing of that. It is answered: the verse contains several rulings, among them the obligation of compensation and its manner. The abrogation affected its manner, not its basis, so it is binding to hold to it. Haram ibn Muhayyisah narrated from his father that the she-camel of al-Bara' entered a man's orchard and damaged it, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ ruled that the owners of property must guard it by day, and the owners of livestock must guard it by night.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We subjected the mountains to glorify [Allah] along with David﴾. The construction of the sentence: "And We subjected the mountains, glorifying with David." Abu Hurayrah said: When he glorified, the mountains and the birds answered him with glorification and remembrance. Others said: when he felt a lull, he commanded the mountains and they glorified, until he longed for it and glorified.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We were the doers﴾; that is, for that. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is: We were capable of what We willed.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We taught him the crafting of armor for you﴾. Regarding the meaning of labus (armor) there are two opinions:

One: the coats of mail; before that they were plates, and David was the first to make these rings and link them together. This was said by Qatadah.

The second: labus means all weapons, from the coat of mail to the spear. This was said by Abu 'Ubaydah. Abu al-Mutawakkil and Ibn al-Sumayfa' recited "lubus" with a damma on the lam.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 21, verses 83–86:

Allah's words: ﴿And Job, when he cried out to his Lord﴾; that is, he called upon his Lord. ﴿"Indeed, adversity has touched me"﴾. Abu Imran al-Jawni recited (إنِّي) with a kasra on the hamza. Hamza recited (مَسَّنِي) with the ya' made sukun; that is, hardship has befallen me. ﴿"And You are the Most Merciful of the merciful"﴾; that is, the most abundant in mercy. This is an indirect way of asking for mercy, since he praised Him by saying He is the Most Merciful, and then fell silent.

**Reference to his story**

The people of tafsir (exegesis) mentioned that Ayyub (peace be upon him) was the wealthiest person of his time and was very generous. Iblis said: "O Lord, give me power over his wealth and his children," and he had thirteen children. "If You do so, You will see how he obeys me and disobeys You." It was said to him: "I have given you power over his wealth and his children." So Iblis returned, gathered his devils and rebellious jinn, and sent some of them to his animals and herdsmen. They seized them until they threw them into the sea. Then Iblis came in the form of his steward and said: "O Ayyub, do you not see that a violent wind has come and carried off your animals and their herdsmen until it cast them into the sea?" He did not answer him until he finished his prayer, then said: "Praise be to Allah, who gave me provision and then took it back from me." So Iblis departed in disappointment. Then he sent some devils to his gardens and crops, and they burned them. He came and informed him, and Ayyub said the same thing. So he sent some devils, who shook the dwellings of Ayyub in which were his sons and servants, and they killed them. He came and informed him. Ayyub praised Allah and said to Iblis, who he thought was his steward regarding his property: "If there were any good in you, He would have taken you with them." So Iblis departed in disappointment. (p. 376) Then it was said to him: "How did you find My servant Ayyub?" He said: "O Lord, give me power over his body, and you will see." It was said to him: "I have given you power over his body." So he came and blew on the big toes of his feet, and they burned like fire. No one in his time wept more than him out of fear of Allah the Exalted. When the trial came upon him, he did not weep, lest it be impatience (jaza') that he feared. His tongue remained busy with remembrance, and his heart with knowledge and gratitude. He could see his intestines, veins and bones. His illness was that all over his body came out warts like the fat tails of sheep, and he was seized with an itching he could not control. He scratched himself with his nails until they fell off, then with coarse woolen garments (masuh), then with stones. His body became foul-smelling and decayed. The people of the town expelled him, and they made him a shelter (arish) on a refuse heap (kunasa). People abandoned him except for his wife, whose name was Rahma bint Ifrayim ibn Yusuf ibn Ya'qub. She used to go to him and bring him what would help him.

Abu Bakr al-Qurashi narrated from al-Layth ibn Sa'd, who said: There was a king who wronged the people. A group of prophets spoke to him about this, but Ayyub remained silent because of horses he had in the king's domain. Allah revealed to him: "Did you leave off speaking to him for the sake of your horses? I will surely prolong your trial."

They differed about the duration of his remaining in the trial, in four opinions:

The first: eighteen years, narrated by Anas ibn Malik from the Prophet (ﷺ).

The second: seven years, said by Ibn Abbas, Ka'b, and Yahya ibn Abi Kathir. (p. 377)

The third: seven years and some months, said by al-Hasan.

The fourth: three years, said by Wahb.

Regarding the reason for his asking for well-being, there are six opinions:

The first: [that] he desired a condiment (idam), but his wife did not get it for him until she sold a lock of her hair. When he learned of this, he said: ﴿"Adversity has touched me"﴾. This was narrated by al-Dahhak from Ibn Abbas.

The second: that Allah made him forget supplication, despite his frequent remembrance of Allah. When the appointed term of the trial ended, He made supplication easy for him, and He answered him. This was narrated by al-Awfi from Ibn Abbas.

The third: that some men from the Children of Israel passed by him, and some of them said to others: "Only a great sin could have caused this to befall him." At that point he said: ﴿"Adversity has touched me"﴾. This was said by Nawf al-Bikali. Abdullah ibn Ubayd ibn Umayr said: He had two brothers who came to him one day and found a foul smell. They said: "If Allah had known any good in him, He would not have brought him to all this." He heard nothing more painful than that. So he said: "O Allah, if You know that I never spent a night full while I knew of a hungry person, then testify for me." He was vindicated while they were listening. Then he said: "O Allah, if You know that I never wore a shirt while I knew of a naked person, then testify for me." He was vindicated while they were listening. Then he fell prostrate and said: "O Allah, I will not raise my head until You remove what is upon me." Allah the Mighty and Majestic removed what was upon him.

The fourth: that Iblis came to his wife with a young goat and said: "Let Ayyub slaughter this for me, now that he is healed." She came and told him. He said: "If Allah heals me, I will flog you a hundred lashes. You commanded me to slaughter for other than Allah!" Then he drove her away from him, and she left. When he saw that he had no food, no drink, and no friend, he fell prostrate and said: ﴿"Adversity has touched me"﴾. This was said by al-Hasan.

The fifth: that Allah the Exalted revealed to him, while he was in the prime of his youth: "I am going to test you." (p. 378) He said: "O Lord, where will my heart be?" He said: "With Me." So He poured upon him the trials you have heard of, until the trial reached its limit. Then He revealed to him: "I will grant you well-being." He said: "O Lord, where will my heart be?" He said: "With you." He said: ﴿"Adversity has touched me"﴾. This was said by Ibrahim ibn Shayban al-Qarmisi, as he related it to us from him.

The sixth: that revelation was cut off from him for forty days, so he feared being forsaken by his Lord, and said: ﴿"Adversity has touched me"﴾. This was mentioned by al-Mawardi.

If it is asked: where is patience, when this is a complaint?

The answer: complaining to Allah does not contradict patience. What is blameworthy is complaining to people. Did you not hear the words of Ya'qub: ﴿"I only complain of my anguish and my grief to Allah"﴾ [Yusuf 12:86]? Sufyan ibn Uyayna said: Likewise, whoever complains to people while, in his complaint, he is content with the decree of Allah, that is not impatience. Did you not hear the words of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to Jibril during his illness: "I find myself distressed," and "I find myself in anguish," and his saying: "Rather, I am in pain, my head!"

Allah's words: ﴿And We gave him his family﴾; meaning his children, ﴿and the like of them with them﴾. On this there are four opinions:

The first: Allah the Exalted restored his family to him in person, and gave him the like of them with them in this world. This was said by Ibn Mas'ud, al-Hasan, and Qatada. Abu Salih narrated from Ibn Abbas: His wife had given birth to seven sons and seven daughters for him, and they were brought back to life for him; and his wife bore him seven sons and seven daughters.

The second: they had been hidden from him and had not died. He gave them back to him in this world and gave him the like of them with them in the Hereafter. This was narrated by Hisham from al-Hasan.

The third: Allah gave him the rewards of his family in the Hereafter, and gave him the like of them in this world. This was said by Nawf and Mujahid.

The fourth: He gave him his family and the like of them with them in the Hereafter. This was related by al-Zajjaj.

Allah's words: ﴿As a mercy from Us﴾; that is, We did that for him as a mercy from Us. ﴿And a reminder﴾; that is, an admonition for the worshippers. Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: Whoever is afflicted with a trial should remember what befell Ayyub, and say: "Indeed, one better than me has been afflicted."

Allah's words: ﴿And Dhu al-Kifl﴾. They differed as to whether he was a prophet or not, on two views:

One of them: he was not a prophet, but was a righteous servant. This was said by Abu Musa al-Ash'ari and Mujahid. Then those who held this view differed about the reason he was called Dhu al-Kifl, in three opinions. The first: a man used to pray one hundred prayers every day, then he died, and he was guaranteed (kafala) through his prayer, so he was called Dhu al-Kifl. This was said by Abu Musa al-Ash'ari. The second: he took on the guarantee (takaffala) for a prophet, regarding his people, that he would take care of their affairs for him, keep them in order, and judge between them justly, and he did so, so he was called Dhu al-Kifl. This was said by Mujahid. The third: a king killed three hundred prophets in one day, and one hundred prophets fled from him. Dhu al-Kifl guaranteed (kafala) them, feeding and giving them drink until they escaped, so he was called Dhu al-Kifl. This was said by Ibn al-Sa'ib.

The second view: he was a prophet. This was said by al-Hasan and Ata'. Ata' said: (p. 380) Allah the Exalted revealed to one of the prophets: "I intend to take your soul, so offer your kingship to the Children of Israel. Whoever guarantees to you that he will pray at night without ceasing, fast by day without breaking his fast, and judge between people without becoming angry, to him give your kingdom." He did so, and a young man stood up and said: "I will guarantee this for you." So he took on the guarantee, and he fulfilled it. Allah thanked him for that and made him a prophet, and he was called Dhu al-Kifl.

Al-Tha'labi mentioned the hadith of Ibn Umar from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about al-Kifl: "He was a man who never refrained from a sin. He was alone with a woman in order to commit adultery with her. She wept and said: 'I have never done this before.' So he got up from her, repentant, and died that very night. In the morning, it was written on his door: 'Allah has forgiven al-Kifl.'" The hadith is well known, and I have mentioned it in al-Hada'iq. Al-Tha'labi made this one of the views on explaining Dhu al-Kifl, but this is an error, because that man's name was al-Kifl, whereas the one mentioned in the Qur'an is called Dhu al-Kifl. Also, al-Kifl died on the night in which he repented, so no long time passed in which he struggled with patience against sins. And if we say he was a prophet, then prophets are protected from such a state. I mentioned this to our shaykh Abu al-Fadl ibn Nasir, may Allah the Exalted have mercy on him, and he agreed with me and said: "This is not that."

Allah's words: ﴿Each of them was of the patient﴾; that is, in obedience to Allah and abstaining from disobeying Him. ﴿And We admitted them into Our mercy﴾. Regarding this mercy, there are three opinions:

One: it is Paradise, said by Ibn Abbas. The second: it is prophethood, said by Muqatil. The third: it is blessing and favor, related by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi.

Allah's words: ﴿And Job, when he cried out to his Lord﴾; that is, he called upon his Lord. ﴿"Indeed, adversity has touched me"﴾. Abu Imran al-Jawni recited (إنِّي) with a kasra on the hamza. One: it is Paradise, said by Ibn Abbas. The second: it is prophethood, said by Muqatil. The third: it is blessing and favor, related by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi.

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 21, verses 87–88:**

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And Dhu'l-Nun﴾ means Yunus ibn Matta (Jonah son of Matthew). *Al-nun* is the fish, and it was attributed to him because it swallowed him.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿When he went off in anger﴾. Ibn Qutayba said: *al-mughadaba* is a *mufa'ala* form, and most *mufa'ala* forms involve two parties, such as *munazara* (debating), *mujadala* (disputing) and *mukhasama* (quarrelling). Sometimes it involves only one party, as in your saying *safartu* (I travelled) and *sharaftu al-amr* (I took on the matter). Here it is of this type. Abu'l-Mutawakkil, Abu'l-Jawza', Asim al-Jahdari and Ibn al-Sumayfa' recited *mughdaban* with a sukun on the ghayn, a fatha on the dad, and no alif.

They differed over whom he was angry with, and there are two views:

The first is that he was angry with his people. This was said by Ibn Abbas and al-Dahhak. Regarding the cause of his anger toward them, there are three views:
One: God revealed to a prophet called Sha'ya: "Go to a king named so-and-so and tell him: send a trustworthy prophet to the Children of Israel." A king had raided the Children of Israel and taken many of them captive. The prophet and the king wanted to send Yunus to that king to speak to him so that he would release them. Yunus said to Sha'ya: "Has God commanded you to send me out?" He said: "No." He said: "Has He named me to you?" He said: "No." He said: "Then there are other prophets here besides me." They insisted on him, so he left in anger at the prophet, the king and his people. This is related from Ibn Abbas, and we have expanded on it in (Yunus 10:98).
Two: he suffered from his people a severe ordeal of harm and denial, so he left them impatiently before they had believed. He did not think that this act would bring upon him the punishment that followed. This was mentioned by Ibn al-Anbari. It is also related from Wahb ibn Munabbih, who said: When the burdens of prophethood were laid upon him, he was unable to bear them and did not endure. (p-382) So he threw them from his hand and fled.
Three: when he threatened them with punishment, they repented and it was lifted from them. He was told: "Return to them." He said: "How can I return when they will find me a liar?" So he went away angry at his people, reproaching his Lord. We have mentioned this in (Yunus 10:98).

The second view is that he went off angry at his Lord. This was said by al-Hasan, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Sha'bi and Urwa. Abu Bakr al-Naqqash said: the meaning is "angry on account of his Lord," and he was angry only because of their rebelliousness and disobedience. Ibn Qutayba said: he was incensed at them because of the long suffering he had endured from their denial, longing for the punishment to descend upon them. So God punished him for disliking that He pardon his people.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and thought that We would not have power over him﴾. Ya'qub recited *yuqaddara* with a damma on the ya' and a shadda on the dal, and also with a fatha. Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Abu'l-Jawza' and Ibn Abi Layla recited *yuqdara* with a raised ya', a sukun on the qaf, and a light dal with a fatha. Abu Imran al-Jawni recited *yaqdira* with a fatha on the ya', a sukun on the qaf, and a light kasra on the dal. Al-Zuhri, Ibn Ya'mur and Humayd ibn Qays recited *nuqaddira* with a raised nun, a fatha on the qaf, and a kasra on the dal with a shadda. Then there are three views regarding it:

One: that We would not decree punishment against him. This was narrated by al-Awfi from Ibn Abbas, and Mujahid, Qatada and al-Dahhak also said it. Al-Farra' said: the meaning of the verse is: "he thought that We would not decree (*nuqaddira*) against him the punishment We had decreed." The Arabs say *qadara* with the meaning of *qaddara*. Abu Sakhr said:

"And that time which has passed will not return. Blessed are You; whatever You decree (*taqdir*) will be, and to You belongs the thanks."

He meant: *ma tuqaddir*. This is the view of al-Zajjaj.

Two: "he thought that We would not restrict him." This was said by Ata'. Ibn Qutayba said: it is said "so-and-so is restricted (*muqaddar*) and straitened (*muqatar*)," and from this is God's saying: ﴿so He restricted his provision﴾ (al-Fajr 89:16), meaning He made it narrow for him. Al-Naqqash said: the meaning is: "he thought that He would not restrict his departure," as if he thought that God had granted him latitude, whether he wished to stay or to leave, and he had not been given permission to leave.

Three: the meaning is: "he thought that he could frustrate his Lord, so that He would not have power over him." This was narrated by Awf from al-Hasan. Ibn Zayd and Sulayman al-Taymi said the meaning is: "Did he think that We would not have power over him?" On this view, it is an interrogative whose alif has been dropped. This view indicates that it is from *qudra* (power), and it cannot be conceived except with the interrogative implied. I know of no way to understand it except as a rhetorical interrogative of denial, its implied sense being: "he did not think of Our inability, so where could he flee from Us?"

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So he called out in the darknesses﴾. There are three views concerning it:

One: they are the darkness of the sea, the darkness of the belly of the fish, and the darkness of the night. This was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Qatada, and most scholars.

Two: a fish came and swallowed the fish that was in his belly, so he called out in the darkness of a fish, then in the darkness of a fish, then in the darkness of the sea. This was said by Salim ibn Abi'l-Ja'd.

Three: they are the darkness of the water, the darkness of the fish's intestine, and the darkness of its belly. This was said by Ibn al-Sa'ib. Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas related from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) that he said: "Indeed I know a word that no one in distress says except that God relieves him of it: the word of my brother Yunus: ﴿He called out in the darknesses, 'There is no god but You; glory be to You; indeed I have been of the wrongdoers.'﴾" Al-Hasan said: this is an acknowledgment by Yunus of his sin and a repentance from his error.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So We answered him﴾, that is, We responded to him. ﴿And We saved him from the distress﴾, that is, from the darknesses. ﴿And thus do We save the believers﴾ when they call upon Us. Abu Bakr related from Asim that he recited *nujji al-mu'minin* with a single nun and a shadda on the jim. Al-Zajjaj said: this is an error with no justification. Abu Ali al-Farisi said: the narrator from Asim made a mistake. This is indicated by his leaving the ya' of *nujji* with a sukun and the accusative of *al-mu'minin*. If it were in the passive form, he would not have left the ya' with a sukun, and he would have made *al-mu'minin* nominative.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 21, verse 89–92:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Lord, do not leave me alone (fardan)﴾; meaning: solitary, without a child. ﴿And You are the best of inheritors﴾; meaning: the best of those who remain alive after the dead.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We made his wife fit for him﴾. Concerning this there are three opinions:

One: she was made fit to bear a child after having been barren. This was said by Ibn Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Qatadah.

The second: there was a certain length in her tongue, meaning abusiveness, and so she was set right. This was said by Ata'. As-Suddi said: she was a sharp-tongued woman, and so her tongue was restrained from him. (p-385)

The third: her character was bad. This was said by Muhammad ibn Ka'b.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed they used to hasten to good deeds﴾; meaning: they would race to obey Allah. Concerning those referred to there are two opinions:

One: Zakariyya, his wife, and Yahya. The second: all the prophets mentioned in this surah.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and they used to call upon Us﴾. Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn Muhaysin recited it as (wa-yad'unana), with a single nun.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿with longing and fear﴾; meaning: longing for what is with Us and fear of Us. Al-A'mash recited (rughban wa-ruhban), with a damma on the two rā's and sukūn on the ghayn and the hā', and both are dialects, like (an-nahal) and (an-nuhl), and (as-saqam) and (as-suqm). ﴿And they were humble before Us﴾; meaning: submissive.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And she who guarded her chastity (ahsanat farjaha)﴾. Concerning this there are two opinions:

One: it refers to the place of the child's emergence, and the meaning is that she protected it from what is not lawful. She was described with chastity only because she had been accused of fornication.

The second: it refers to the collar of her garment, and the meaning of farj in the language is every gap between two things, and the place of the collar of a woman's garment is slit, so it is called a farj. This is more eloquent in praise of her, because if she guarded the collar of her garment, she is all the more protective of herself.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So We breathed into it﴾; meaning: We commanded Jibril, and he breathed into her garment, and We caused the spirit of Jesus to enter her just as the wind moves by blowing. He attributed the Spirit to Himself with the attribution of ownership, for honour and distinction. ﴿And We made her and her son a sign﴾. His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, this community of yours is one community﴾. Ibn Abbas said: what is meant by "community" here is the religion. Concerning those referred to there are two opinions:

The second: they are the prophets, peace be upon them, as said by Abu Sulayman ad-Dimashqi.
