One: it refers to the place of the child's emergence, and the meaning is that she protected it from what is not lawful. She was described with chastity only because she had been accused of fornication.

The second: it refers to the collar of her garment, and the meaning of farj in the language is every gap between two things, and the place of the collar of a woman's garment is slit, so it is called a farj. This is more eloquent in praise of her, because if she guarded the collar of her garment, she is all the more protective of herself.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So We breathed into it﴾; meaning: We commanded Jibril, and he breathed into her garment, and We caused the spirit of Jesus to enter her just as the wind moves by blowing. He attributed the Spirit to Himself with the attribution of ownership, for honour and distinction. ﴿And We made her and her son a sign﴾. Az-Zajjaj said: since their situation was one, the sign in both of them was one sign, namely birth without a male. Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn Abi Abla recited (ayatayn), in the dual. 

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, this community of yours is one community﴾. Ibn Abbas said: what is meant by "community" here is the religion. Concerning those referred to there are two opinions:

One: they are the community of Muhammad (ﷺ), and this is the meaning of Muqatil's statement.

The second: they are the prophets, peace be upon them, as said by Abu Sulayman ad-Dimashqi. Then he mentioned the People of the Book, censuring them for their disagreement, and Exalted is He said: ﴿But they cut their affair into sects among themselves﴾; meaning: they differed regarding the religion. ﴿So whoever does righteous deeds﴾; meaning: any of the obligations and acts of righteousness, ﴿his effort will not be denied﴾; meaning: We will not deny what he did, as said by Ibn Qutaybah, and the meaning is that it is accepted from him and he is rewarded for it. ﴿And indeed, We are recording it for him﴾; We command the guardian angels to record it so that We may recompense him for it.

The commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 21, verses 93–100:

Allah's words: ﴿And it is forbidden upon a town﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, and Hafs on the authority of 'Asim read *wa-ḥarām* with an alif. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Abu Bakr on the authority of 'Asim read *wa-ḥirm* with a kasra on the ḥā' and without an alif. Both are dialectal forms (lughatān), and it is said: ḥirm and ḥarām. Mu'adh al-Qari, Abu al-Mutawakkil, and Abu 'Imran al-Jawni read *ḥarm* with a fatḥah on the ḥā', a sukun on the rā', without an alif, and with the mīm in the nominative and tanwin. Sa'id ibn Jubayr read *wa-ḥarma* with a fatḥah on the ḥā', a sukun on the rā', and a fatḥah on the mīm, without tanwin and without an alif. Abu al-Jawza', 'Ikrimah, and al-Ḍaḥḥak read *wa-ḥarima* with fatḥahs on the ḥā' and mīm and a kasra on the rā', without tanwin and without an alif. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, Abu Mijlaz, and Abu Raja' read *wa-ḥaruma* with a fatḥah on the ḥā', a ḍammah on the rā', and a naṣb on the mīm, without an alif.

Regarding the meaning of Allah's words ﴿ḥarām﴾, there are two views:

The first: it means obligatory (wājib). This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, and they cited verses for its meaning:

Indeed I do not see a lamenting person weeping forever over his grief
except that I weep over 'Amr.

That is, obligatory.

The second: it means resolve ('azm). This was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr. 'Ata' said: it is a decree (ḥatm) from Allah. The word "town" (qaryah) refers to its people.

Then, regarding the meaning of the verse, there are four views:

The first: it is obligatory upon a town which We have destroyed that its people will not repent. This was narrated by 'Ikrimah from Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: it is obligatory upon it that when it is destroyed, it does not return to its worldly life. This is the view of Qatadah, and something similar has been narrated from Ibn 'Abbas.

The third: the particle *lā* is redundant (zā'idah), and the meaning is: it is forbidden for a destroyed town that they return to the world. This was said by Ibn Jurayj and Ibn Qutaybah, among others.

The fourth: the statement is connected to what precedes it, because when Allah said ﴿so there is no denial of his effort﴾, He informed us that He has forbidden the acceptance of the deeds of the disbelievers. So the meaning of the verse is: it is forbidden for a town which We have destroyed that any deed of theirs be accepted, because they do not repent. This is the view of al-Zajjaj.

If it is asked: how is it valid that something which is not of a person's own action be forbidden for him, when their return after death is not up to them?

The answer: the meaning is that they are prevented from that, just as a person is prevented from what is forbidden even if he is capable of it. So the comparison with prohibition applies to both situations in terms of prevention.

Allah's words: ﴿until, when Gog and Magog are released﴾. Ibn 'Amir read *futtiḥat* with the shaddah (futtiḥat), and the meaning is that the barrier (radm) is opened for them. ﴿And they, from every hill﴾. Ibn Qutaybah said: from every elevation of the earth and mound. ﴿they race down﴾ from *al-nasalān*, which is closely following the stride with haste, like the walk of a wolf when it hastens; *al-'asalān* is similar to it. Al-Zajjaj said: *al-ḥadab* is every mound, and *yanslūn* means they hasten. Abu Raja' al-'Utaridi and 'Asim al-Jahdari read *yanzulūn* with a ḍammah on the sīn.

Regarding Allah's words ﴿they﴾, there are two views:

The first: it refers to Gog and Magog. This is the view of the majority.

The second: it refers to all of mankind, and the meaning is: they will be gathered to the place of standing. This was said by Mujahid. The first is more correct.

If it is asked: where is the response (jawāb) of ﴿until﴾? There are two views concerning it:

The first: it is Allah's words ﴿and the true promise draws near﴾, and the *wāw* in His words ﴿and drew near﴾ is redundant. This was said by al-Farra'. He said: similar to it is ﴿until, when they reach it and its gates are opened﴾ [Surah al-Zumar: 73], and His words ﴿And when they had both submitted and he had put him down upon his temple﴾, ﴿and We called to him﴾ [Surah al-Saffat: 103–104], the meaning being: We called. 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud said: the Hour, among people after Gog and Magog, is like a pregnant woman near term, whose people do not know when it will surprise them with its child, at night or by day.

The second: it is an omitted statement in His words ﴿O woe to us!﴾, so the meaning is: until, when Gog and Magog are released and the promise draws near, they will say: O woe to us! Al-Zajjaj said: this is the view of the Basrans. As for ﴿the true promise﴾, it is the Resurrection.

Allah's words ﴿then behold﴾. Regarding *hiya* in this phrase, there are four views:

The first: *hiya* is a reference back to the eyes (abṣār), and "the eyes" is its explanation, like the words of the poet:

By the life of her father, my litter-companion does not say: "Has Malik ibn Abi Ka'b not fled from me?"

Here he mentioned the litter-companion (ẓa'īnah), and had referred to her in "by the life of her father."

The second: *hiya* is a separating pronoun (ḍamīr al-faṣl) and a support (*'imād*), and *huwa* could fill its position. Similar to it is His words ﴿Indeed, it is I, Allah﴾ [Surah al-Naml: 9], and His words ﴿for indeed, it is not the eyes that are blinded﴾ [Surah al-Hajj: 46]. They cited:

With a garment, a dinar, a sheep, and a dirham, is there a head (ra's) raised by what is here?

Al-Farra' mentioned both of these.

The third: the complete statement ends at *hiya*, meaning: then behold, it is exposed and standing, that is, due to its nearness, as if it is coming and present. Then he began a new statement, saying ﴿fixed﴾. Al-Tha'labi mentioned this.

The fourth: *hiya* is a reference back to the matter (al-qiṣṣah), and the meaning is: the matter is that their eyes are fixed on that day. Al-Naysaburi, 'Ali ibn Ahmad, mentioned this. The exegetes said: the eyes of the disbelievers will stare from the terror of the Day of Resurrection, and they will say ﴿O woe to us! We were﴾, that is, in the world, ﴿in heedlessness of this﴾, that is, of it, ﴿rather, we were wrongdoers﴾ against ourselves by our disbelief and disobedience. Then He addressed the people of Makkah, saying ﴿Indeed, you and what you worship besides Allah﴾, meaning: the idols, ﴿are fuel (ḥaṣab) for Hell﴾. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, Abu al-'Aliyah, and 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz read *ḥaṭab* with the ṭā'. Ibn 'Abbas, 'A'ishah, and Ibn al-Sumayfa' read *ḥaḍab* with an unpointed (mu'jamah) ḍād with fatḥah. 'Urwah, 'Ikrimah, Ibn Ya'mur, and Ibn Abi 'Ablah read *ḥaḍb* with a sukun on the ḍād. Abu al-Mutawakkil, Abu Hayawah, and Mu'adh al-Qari read *ḥiḍb* with a kasra on the ḥā' and a sukun on the ḍād. Abu Mijlaz, Abu Raja', and Ibn Muhaysin read *ḥaṣb* with a fatḥah on the ḥā' and an unpointed ṣād with a sukun. Al-Zajjaj said: whoever reads *ḥaṣab Jahannam*, its meaning is everything which is thrown into it; whoever reads *ḥaṭab*, its meaning is that with which it is kindled; and whoever reads with the pointed ḍād, its meaning is that with which the fire is agitated and kindled. Ibn Qutaybah said: *al-ḥaṣab* is what is cast into it, and its origin is from *al-ḥaṣbā'*, which is pebbles. It is said: "I pelted so-and-so" (ḥaṣabtu fulānan) when you pelt him with pebbles, with a sukun on the ṣād; and what you pelt with is *ḥaṣab*, with a fatḥah on the ṣād.

Allah's words ﴿you﴾ refer to the worshippers and the worshipped, ﴿are to it arriving﴾, that is, entering. ﴿Had these been gods﴾, meaning the idols, ﴿in reality﴾, ﴿they would not have entered it﴾. Regarding this there are three views:

The first: it refers to the idols, and the meaning is: had they been gods, they would not have entered the Fire.

The second: it refers to their worshippers, and the meaning is: had the idols been gods, they would have prevented their worshippers from entering the Fire.

The third: it refers to the gods and their worshippers, as evidenced by His words ﴿and all therein will abide forever﴾, meaning the worshipper and the worshipped.

Allah's words ﴿For them therein is a roaring (zafīr)﴾. We have already explained the meaning of *al-zafīr* in (Hud: 106). Regarding the reason for their not hearing, there are three views:

The first: nails of fire are placed in their ears, then they are cast into coffins of fire which are sealed over them. This was narrated by Abu Umamah from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in a lengthy hadith. Ibn Mas'ud said: when those who will remain in the Fire forever remain in it, they are placed in coffins of fire, then those coffins are placed inside other coffins, so they hear nothing, and none of them sees that there is anyone in the Fire being punished other than himself.

The second: hearing is a comfort (uns), and Allah does not love to comfort them. This was said by 'Awn ibn 'Umarah.

The third: they do not hear only because of the intense boiling of Hell. This was said by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi.

Al-Farra' mentioned both of these.

The commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 21, verses 93–100:

Allah's words: ﴿And it is forbidden upon a town﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, and Hafs on the authority of 'Asim read *wa-ḥarām* with an alif. Mu'adh al-Qari, Abu al-Mutawakkil, and Abu 'Imran al-Jawni read *ḥarm* with a fatḥah on the ḥā', a sukun on the rā', without an alif, and with the mīm in the nominative and tanwin. Sa'id ibn Jubayr read *wa-ḥarma* with a fatḥah on the ḥā', a sukun on the rā', and a fatḥah on the mīm, without tanwin and without an alif. Abu al-Jawza', 'Ikrimah, and al-Ḍaḥḥak read *wa-ḥarima* with fatḥahs on the ḥā' and mīm and a kasra on the rā', without tanwin and without an alif. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, Abu Mijlaz, and Abu Raja' read *wa-ḥaruma* with a fatḥah on the ḥā', a ḍammah on the rā', and a naṣb on the mīm, without an alif.

The first: it means obligatory (wājib). This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, and they cited verses for its meaning:

Indeed I do not see a lamenting person weeping forever over his grief
except that I weep over 'Amr.

That is, obligatory.

The first: it is obligatory upon a town which We have destroyed that its people will not repent. This was narrated by 'Ikrimah from Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: it is obligatory upon it that when it is destroyed, it does not return to its worldly life. This is the view of Qatadah, and something similar has been narrated from Ibn 'Abbas.

The third: the particle *lā* is redundant (zā'idah), and the meaning is: it is forbidden for a destroyed town that they return to the world. This was said by Ibn Jurayj and Ibn Qutaybah, among others.

The answer: the meaning is that they are prevented from that, just as a person is prevented from what is forbidden even if he is capable of it. So the comparison with prohibition applies to both situations in terms of prevention.

The second: hearing is a comfort (uns), and Allah does not love to comfort them. This was said by 'Awn ibn 'Umarah.

Then He addressed the people of Makkah, saying ﴿Indeed, you and what you worship besides Allah﴾, meaning: the idols, ﴿are fuel (ḥaṣab) for Hell﴾. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, Abu al-'Aliyah, and 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz read *ḥaṭab* with the ṭā'. Ibn 'Abbas, 'A'ishah, and Ibn al-Sumayfa' read *ḥaḍab* with an unpointed (mu'jamah) ḍād with fatḥah. 'Urwah, 'Ikrimah, Ibn Ya'mur, and Ibn Abi 'Ablah read *ḥaḍb* with a sukun on the ḍād. Abu al-Mutawakkil, Abu Hayawah, and Mu'adh al-Qari read *ḥiḍb* with a kasra on the ḥā' and a sukun on the ḍād. Abu Mijlaz, Abu Raja', and Ibn Muhaysin read *ḥaṣb* with a fatḥah on the ḥā' and an unpointed ṣād with a sukun. Al-Zajjaj said: whoever reads *ḥaṣab Jahannam*, its meaning is everything which is thrown into it; whoever reads *ḥaṭab*, its meaning is that with which it is kindled; and whoever reads with the pointed ḍād, its meaning is that with which the fire is agitated and kindled. Ibn Qutaybah said: *al-ḥaṣab* is what is cast into it, and its origin is from *al-ḥaṣbā'*, which is pebbles. It is said: "I pelted so-and-so" (ḥaṣabtu fulānan) when you pelt him with pebbles, with a sukun on the ṣād; and what you pelt with is *ḥaṣab*, with a fatḥah on the ṣād.

Allah's words ﴿you﴾ refer to the worshippers and the worshipped, ﴿are to it arriving﴾, that is, entering. ﴿Had these been gods﴾, meaning the idols, ﴿in reality﴾, ﴿they would not have entered it﴾. Regarding this there are three views:

The first: it refers to the idols, and the meaning is: had they been gods, they would not have entered the Fire.

The second: it refers to their worshippers, and the meaning is: had the idols been gods, they would have prevented their worshippers from entering the Fire.

The third: it refers to the gods and their worshippers, as evidenced by His words ﴿and all therein will abide forever﴾, meaning the worshipper and the worshipped.

Allah's words ﴿For them therein is a roaring (zafīr)﴾. We have already explained the meaning of *al-zafīr* in (Hud: 106). Regarding the reason for their not hearing, there are three views:

The first: nails of fire are placed in their ears, then they are cast into coffins of fire which are sealed over them. This was narrated by Abu Umamah from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in a lengthy hadith. Ibn Mas'ud said: when those who will remain in the Fire forever remain in it, they are placed in coffins of fire, then those coffins are placed inside other coffins, so they hear nothing, and none of them sees that there is anyone in the Fire being punished other than himself.

The second: hearing is a comfort (uns), and Allah does not love to comfort them. This was said by 'Awn ibn 'Umarah.

The third: they do not hear only because of the intense boiling of Hell. This was said by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi.

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 21, verses 101–107**

Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿Indeed, those for whom the best [reward] has already preceded from Us﴾. The occasion of its revelation (sabab al-nuzul) is that when ﴿Indeed, you and what you worship besides Allah are the fuel of Hell﴾ was revealed, this was difficult for the Quraysh, and they said: "He has reviled our gods." Then Ibn al-Zib'ara came and said: "What is wrong with you?" They said: "He has reviled our gods." He said: "What did he say?" So they informed him. He said: "Call him to me." When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was summoned, [Ibn al-Zib'ara] said: "O Muhammad, is this specific to our gods, or to everyone who is worshipped besides Allah?" He said: "No, rather it is for everyone who is worshipped besides Allah." Ibn al-Zib'ara said: "You have been defeated, by the Lord of this House! Do you not claim that the angels are righteous servants, and that Jesus is a righteous servant, and that 'Uzayr is a righteous servant? Yet these are the Banu Mulayh who worship the angels, these are the Christians who worship Jesus, and these are the Jews who worship 'Uzayr." Then the people of Makkah raised an outcry, and this verse was revealed. This was related by Ibn 'Abbas.

Al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl said: By His saying ﴿what you worship﴾ He only meant the idols, to the exclusion of others, because had He intended the angels and people He would have said "man" (من). It has also been said that "inna" here means "illa" (except), so the meaning is: "except those for whom the best [reward] has already preceded from Us." This is the recitation of Ibn Mas'ud and Abu Nuhayk, for both of them recited: "illa alladhina" (except those who). It is also related from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib that he recited this verse and said: "I am among them, and Abu Bakr, 'Umar, 'Uthman, Talhah, al-Zubayr, Sa'd and 'Abd al-Rahman."

Regarding what is meant by "al-husna" (the best), there are two opinions: the first is Paradise, related by Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ikrimah; the second is happiness, related by Ibn Zayd.

Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿They will be kept far from it﴾; that is, far from Hell, whose mention has already preceded. ﴿Far away (mub'adun)﴾: "bu'd" is the great length of distance. "Hasis" is the sound that you hear from a thing when it passes near you. Ibn 'Abbas said: The people of Paradise will not hear the hasis of the people of the Fire when they have come down to their places in Paradise.

Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿The greatest terror will not grieve them﴾. Abu Razin, Qatadah, Ibn Abi 'Abla, Ibn Muhaysin, and Abu Ja'far al-Shaizari, from al-Kisa'i, recited: "la yuhzinuhum" with a damma on the ya' and a kasra on the zay' (a recitation variant, qira'a).

Regarding "the greatest terror" there are four opinions:
The first is that it is the final blast (of the Trumpet); this was narrated by al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas, and by this blast people rise from their graves. What confirms this view is Allah's saying: ﴿and the angels will receive them﴾.
The second is that it is the closing of the Fire upon its inhabitants; this was narrated by Sa'id ibn Jubayr from Ibn 'Abbas, and al-Dahhak said the same.
The third is that it is the slaughtering of Death between Paradise and the Fire; this too is related from Ibn 'Abbas, and Ibn Jurayj said the same.
The fourth is that it is when the servant is commanded to be taken to the Fire; this was said by al-Hasan al-Basri.

Regarding the place where the angels will receive them, there are two opinions: the first is when they rise from their graves, said by Muqatil; the second is at the gates of Paradise, said by Ibn al-Sa'ib.

Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿This is your day﴾. There is an implied element in it: [they] will say, "This is your day," ﴿which you were promised﴾, namely Paradise.

Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿On the day We roll up the heaven﴾. Abu al-'Aliyah, Ibn Abi 'Abla and Abu Ja'far recited: "tuta" with a damma on the initial ta' and "al-sama'u" with a raf' (nominative), i.e., "the heaven is rolled up." That means the erasing of its traces, the dimming of its stars, and the folding up of its sun. ﴿Like the rolling of the scroll for the writings﴾. The majority recited "al-sijilli" with a kasra on the sin and the jim and a shaddah on the lam. Al-Hasan, Abu al-Mutawakkil, (a recitation variant), Abu al-Jawza', and Mahbub from Abu 'Amr recited "al-sijli" with a kasra on the sin and a light sukun on the jim. Abu al-Sammak recited likewise, except that he put a fatha on the jim.

Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿for the writings﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir recited "lil-kitab" (singular). Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Hafs from 'Asim recited "lil-kutub" (plural).

Regarding "al-sijjil" there are four opinions:
The first is that it is an angel; this was said by 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, Ibn 'Umar and al-Suddi.
The second is that it was a scribe of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ); this was narrated by Abu al-Jawza' from Ibn 'Abbas.
The third is that "al-sijjil" means "the man"; Abu al-Jawza' narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "al-sijjil is the man." Our shaykh Abu Mansur the linguist said: It has been said that "al-sijjil" in the language of Abyssinia means "the man."
The fourth is that it is the page (sahifah); this was narrated by Ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn 'Abbas, and Mujahid, al-Farra' and Ibn Qutaybah said the same. I read to our shaykh Abu Mansur, who said: Abu Bakr, meaning Ibn Durayd, said: "al-sijjil" is the book, and Allah knows best. I do not pay attention to their saying that it is a Persian word that has been Arabized. The meaning is: just as the scroll is folded over what is in it of writing. The "lam" here means "upon." Some scholars said: What is meant by "the writing" is "the written," so when the written is folded along with the folding of the page, the scroll is made as if it were folding the writing.

Then He resumed, saying: ﴿As We began the first creation, We shall repeat it﴾. Here "al-khalq" is a verbal noun (masdar), not a meaning of "the created thing" (makhluq).

Regarding the meaning of the statement there are four opinions:
The first is: just as We began them in the wombs of their mothers, barefoot, naked and uncircumcised, so We shall return them on the Day of Resurrection. This was related from Ibn 'Abbas, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), that he said: "People will be gathered on the Day of Resurrection naked, barefoot and uncircumcised, as they were created," and then he recited: ﴿As We began the first creation, We shall repeat it﴾. Mujahid went to this meaning.
The second is that the meaning is: We will destroy everything as it was the first time; this was narrated by al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas.
The third is that the sky will rain for forty days like the semen of men, and they will sprout by the rain in their graves as they sprout in the wombs of their mothers; this was narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas.
The fourth is that the meaning is: Our power to repeat is like Our power to begin; this was said by al-Zajjaj.

Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿as a promise﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: It is in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar), because His saying ﴿We shall repeat it﴾ means: "We promised this as a promise." ﴿Indeed We are ever doers﴾; that is, capable of doing whatever We will. Others said: "Indeed We are ever doers of what We have promised."

Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿And We had certainly written in the Zabur after the Reminder﴾. Regarding this there are four opinions:
The first is that the Zabur is all the books sent down from heaven, and the Reminder is the Mother of the Book that is with Allah; this was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr in one narration, and by Mujahid and Ibn Zayd, and this is the meaning of the statement of Ibn 'Abbas in the narration of Ibn Jubayr, for he said: "The Zabur is the Torah, the Gospel and the Qur'an, and the Reminder is the one that is in heaven."
The second is that the Zabur is the books and the Reminder is the Torah; this was narrated by al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas.
The third is that the Zabur is the Qur'an and the Reminder is the Torah and the Gospel; this was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr in one narration.
The fourth is that the Zabur is the Psalms of Dawud, and the Reminder is the mention of Musa; this was said by al-Sha'bi.

Regarding the earth mentioned here there are three opinions:
The first is that it is the earth of Paradise; this was narrated by Sa'id ibn Jubayr from Ibn 'Abbas, and most scholars said the same.
The second is the earth of this world; this too is reported from Ibn 'Abbas.
The third is the Holy Land; this was said by Ibn al-Sa'ib.

Regarding His saying ﴿My righteous servants will inherit it﴾ there are three opinions:
The first is that they are the Ummah of Muhammad (ﷺ); this was narrated by Ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn 'Abbas, and in one narration: "The Ummah of Muhammad will inherit the earth of this world through conquests."
The second is the Children of Israel; this was said by Ibn al-Sa'ib.
The third is that it is general for every righteous person; this was said by some of the jurists among the exegetes.

Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿Indeed, in this﴾, meaning the Qur'an, ﴿is a message (balaghan)﴾; that is, a sufficiency. The meaning is: whoever follows the Qur'an and acts by it, the Qur'an will be his means of reaching Paradise.

Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿for a people who worship﴾. Ka'b said: They are the Ummah of Muhammad (ﷺ) who perform the five prayers and fast the month of Ramadan.

Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿And We have not sent you except as a mercy to the worlds﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: This is general for the righteous and the wicked. Whoever believes in him, the mercy is completed for him in this world and the Hereafter; and whoever disbelieves in him, the punishment is averted from him until death and the Resurrection. Ibn Zayd said: He is a mercy specifically for whoever believes in him.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 21, verses 108–112:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So will you submit?﴾ Ibn ʿAbbas said: "Will you then single Him out in worship?" The scholars of meanings (ahl al-maʿani) said: "This is a question with the meaning of a command."

The first: "I have declared hostility toward you, opposed you, and informed you of this, so that I and you are on equal terms, having equal knowledge of it." This is a concise form of speech, as said by Ibn Qutaybah.

The second: "I have informed you through the revelation made to me, so that you may be equal in belief in it," as said by al-Zajjaj.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And I do not know﴾; that is, I do not know ﴿whether what you are promised is near or far﴾, namely the descent of the punishment upon you. ﴿Indeed, He knows what is spoken aloud﴾, which is what they say to the Prophet ﷺ: ﴿When is this promise?﴾ [Yasin: 48], ﴿and what you conceal﴾, their secret conviction that the punishment will not occur.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, it is a trial for you﴾. Regarding the pronoun in ﴿la-ʿallahu﴾ (it may be) there are two views:

The first: that it refers to what He has announced to them, as said by al-Zajjaj.

The meaning of "fitna" (trial) here is testing. ﴿And enjoyment for a time﴾; that is, you enjoy yourselves until the end of your lifespans.

The meaning according to this is: decide between me and the polytheists (p-400) by that which makes the truth manifest. The meaning of ﴿against what you describe﴾ is: against your lies and falsehood. The first: "I have declared hostility toward you, opposed you, and informed you of this, so that I and you are on equal terms, having equal knowledge of it." This is a concise form of speech, as said by Ibn Qutaybah.

The second: "I have informed you through the revelation made to me, so that you may be equal in belief in it," as said by al-Zajjaj.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And I do not know﴾; that is, I do not know ﴿whether what you are promised is near or far﴾, namely the descent of the punishment upon you. ﴿Indeed, He knows what is spoken aloud﴾, which is what they say to the Prophet ﷺ: ﴿When is this promise?﴾ [Yasin: 48], ﴿and what you conceal﴾, their secret conviction that the punishment will not occur.

The second: that it refers to the punishment, so the meaning is: perhaps the delay of the punishment for you is a trial, as said by Ibn Jarir and Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi. The meaning of "fitna" (trial) here is testing. ﴿And enjoyment for a time﴾; that is, you enjoy yourselves until the end of your lifespans.
